decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt The original study’s main finding, a significant effect of explanation level, did not replciate (p = .376). Additionally, the main effect of explanation quality, a particularly strong effect in the original paper, did not replicate either (p = .062). In terms of robustness, an effect of explanation level was only found for psychological explanations (p = .043), although it went in the opposite direction from what was predicted, contradicting both the original study and the seductive allure effect that Hopkins et al (2016) was based on.

decisions.reason: In the primary replication report for Hopkins, Weisberg, & Taylor (2016) (hopkins2016.html, line 566), the author explicitly concludes that the original study's main finding (the effect of explanation level on explanation rating) did not replicate (b = 0.14, 95% CI [-0.18, 0.47], p = .376) and that the main effect of explanation quality also did not replicate (p = .062); raw_data.csv (line 350) likewise records replication codes of 0 and 0. The overall replication outcome is therefore failed.

decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt This replication was a success. The key statistic of interest was the main effect of congruency in the 2x2 ANOVA with task and congruency as factors. The original study found main effect of congruency, F(1, 15) = 14.3, p = 0.002, and our replication found a main effect of congruency, F(1,15) = 13.2, p = 0.003.

decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt The original finding was that participants in the responsive condition had significantly higher global processing scores (12.27 trials) than participants in the unresponsive condition (10.51 trials), p = .0006. This primary statistical test did not replicate. I ran a t-test between the unresponsive and responsive conditions, and my findings showed the opposite trend. The responsive condition had a lower mean global processing score (9.45 trials) than the responsive condition (10.34 trials). Additionally, the difference between these groups was not statistically significant, although this is unsurprising given that we were 80% powered (a priori) to detect an effect size of approximately d = .37, and we found an effect size of d = -.2.
